question: A 63-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his wife because she is concerned he is having another stroke. The patient says he woke up with right-sided facial weakness and drooping. Past medical history is significant for a recent case of shingles treated with acyclovir, and a stroke, diagnosed 10 years ago, from which he recovered with no residual functional deficits. On physical examination, there is weakness and drooping of the entire right side of the face. Sensation is intact. The remainder of the physical examination is unremarkable. Which of the following additional findings would also most likely be seen in this patient?

options.opc: Complete loss of taste to the tongue

enhanced_information: The patient's presentation of right-sided facial weakness and drooping suggests a lower motor neuron lesion of the facial nerve, typically affecting all branches. This would result in an inability to wrinkle the forehead on the affected side, consistent with clinical expectations of such a lesion. Other symptoms like partial hearing loss or complete loss of taste are less directly correlated with typical presentations of isolated facial nerve involvement.
analysis: The patient's symptoms suggest a lower motor neuron lesion of the facial nerve, typically affecting all branches including those to the forehead. This results in an inability to wrinkle the forehead on the affected side, which is consistent with the medical consensus on such lesions.
